procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge, Special Fast Track Court, Dwarka Courts, New Delhi (Sessions Court) in Sessions Case No. 67/2015.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 30.09.2016 passed by the High Court of Delhi in Criminal Appeal No.46/2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Delhi, in Criminal Appeal No. 46/2016, modified the judgment and order dated 27.11.2015 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant-accused appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's judgment and order dated 30.09.2016. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sexual relationship was consensual or if the consent was vitiated by a false promise of marriage, constituting rape under Section 376 IPC.
appellant_arguments: The physical relationship with the prosecutrix was consensual.
The prosecutrix was aware that he was a married person with children and had even met his wife.
He was providing regular financial help to the prosecutrix.
The prosecutrix lodged a false case against him after he refused to fulfill her demand for Rs. 1.5 lakh to Rs. 2 lakhs.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the Sessions Court and the High Court which held the appellant guilty.
The appellant lured the prosecutrix into a sexual relationship by giving her a false promise of marriage.
The appellant committed a breach of the promise after she delivered a child, which proves her consent was obtained under a misconception of fact.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: There is no straitjacket formula for determining whether consent given to sexual intercourse is voluntary or given under a misconception of fact. The court must, in each case, consider the specific evidence and surrounding circumstances to reach a conclusion, as the burden is on the prosecution to prove the absence of consent.
obiter: The consensus of judicial opinion is that consent given to sexual intercourse with a person with whom the prosecutrix is deeply in love, on a promise of future marriage, cannot be said to be given under a misconception of fact.
A false promise is not a fact within the meaning of the Code.

The law declared by this Court provides guidelines to the judicial mind, but courts while applying the law must also consider the evidence before them and the surrounding circumstances under which the alleged offences are committed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The application of established law regarding consent in rape cases is not a mechanical process; it is fundamentally dependent on the specific, proven facts and surrounding circumstances of each individual case. While prior judgments provide guidelines, the court must weigh the unique legal evidence presented before it to determine whether consent was voluntary or vitiated by a misconception of fact.
legal_tests_applied: The prosecution bears the burden to prove each and every ingredient of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt, and the absence of consent is one such essential ingredient.

The court must determine if the consent given by the prosecutrix was under a misconception of fact as contemplated by Section 90 of the IPC, which would bring the act within the scope of rape under Section 375 IPC.
The application of legal precedent (the ratio laid down in judgments) must be tailored to the proved facts and surrounding circumstances of the specific case at hand.
policy_considerations: While adhering to the criminal jurisprudence principle that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the court must also consider the ethos and culture of Indian society and the rising incidence of the social crime of rape.
